seo_title: Yawning Gape: Pacific Sleeper Sharks Swallow Large Prey Whole
fact_hook: A massive shark engulfs prey nearly its own size in darkness.
fact_explanation: Pacific sleeper sharks possess large mouths and suction-feeding capability, enabling them to ingest substantial prey items, including large fish and marine mammals, in low-visibility deep waters.
impact_paragraph_1: In habitats where chasing prey is inefficient, a wide gape and powerful suction allow a slow-moving predator to seize sizable animals weighing hundreds of kilograms.
impact_paragraph_2: This feeding strategy supports the maintenance of extreme body size in food-limited ecosystems, where capturing a single large prey item can sustain a giant predator for extended periods.
did_you_know: Suction feeding is a common strategy among deep-sea fishes operating in low-light conditions.
subject: Pacific Sleeper Shark
source: Alaska Department of Fish and Game

seo_title: Zero-Light Navigation: Pacific Sleeper Sharks Rely on Non-Visual Senses
fact_hook: This giant predator hunts where sight becomes nearly useless.
fact_explanation: At depths beyond 2,000 meters, Pacific sleeper sharks operate in the aphotic zone, relying on sensory systems such as electroreception and olfaction rather than vision to locate prey.
impact_paragraph_1: In total darkness, detecting faint electrical signals and chemical traces becomes more valuable than eyesight, allowing a bus-length shark to pinpoint living or dead prey in vast black waters.
impact_paragraph_2: This sensory adaptation demonstrates how apex predators evolve alternative detection systems when light vanishes, enabling dominance in environments that appear inhospitable to large hunters.
did_you_know: All sharks possess electroreceptors called ampullae of Lorenzini to sense electrical fields.
subject: Pacific Sleeper Shark
